claims.source: From a selection of independently isolated KPC-derived cell lines, we first determined the cell line KPC-F as an appropriate model for human PDAC tumor based on the expression of epithelial (E-cadherin), mesenchymal (vimentin), and stromal (Collagen I, αSMA) markers as well as displaying growth kinetics (determined by MRI) amenable for the study and expression of high levels of CCL5 (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: CCR5i treatment significantly reduces Treg infiltration in orthotopic PDAC tumors.
claims.source: Mice in the CCR5i-treated group showed a trend toward reduction in NK cells and all T-cell subsets with a significant reduction in Treg (Live/CD45+CD3+CD4+FOXP3+) infiltration, indicating the active recruitment of CCR5+ Tregs in PDAC (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Standalone inhibition of CCR5 is unlikely to clinically benefit PDAC progression.
claims.source: Given the enhanced effect of CCR5i on tumor growth kinetics (Figure 3A), however, standalone inhibition of CCR5 is unlikely to clinically benefit PDAC progression.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from tumor growth data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: IR/CCR5i/αPD1 triple combination treatment significantly reduces p53+ KPC cells compared to all other conditions.
claims.source: Moreover, IR/CCR5i/αPD1-treated tumor sections had significantly reduced DAPI+ and p53+ KPC cells compared to all other conditions, suggesting significantly more loss of tumor cells by triple combination treatment (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Triple combination treatment demonstrated increased necrotic areas over standalone radiotherapy.
claims.source: Tumor sections from the triple combination treatment also presented with increased loss of active stroma (αSMA staining, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and increased necrotic areas over standalone radiotherapy (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3C and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Triple combination treatment demonstrated infiltration of CD8+ T-cells into the center of tumors.
claims.source: In line with apparent increased tumor control, the triple combination treatment demonstrated infiltration of CD8+ T-cells (Figure 3D), supporting greater penetration of CD8+ T-cells into the center of tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3D and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The triple combination reduced Treg infiltration and enhanced CD8+ T-cell infiltration.
claims.source: In line with the results above, the triple combination reduced Treg infiltration, enhanced CD8+ T-cell infiltration, and supported a moderate increase in CD4+ T helper cells (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: A significant infiltration of NK and NKT cells was observed with IR/CCR5i/αPD1 combination treatment.
claims.source: Interestingly, no alteration was seen in the myeloid compartment, except for a reduced infiltration of PMN-MDSCs, whereas a significant infiltration of NK and NKT cells could be observed in pairwise comparisons between IR+αPD1 vs IR+CCR5i or IR/CCR5i/αPD1 (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: CD8 T-cells and NK cells show a significant inverse correlation with E-cadherin+ cells.
claims.source: To correlate immune infiltration against loss of tumor cells (a measure of local tumor control), we determined relationships between CD4 T-, CD8 T-, and NK cell populations and E-cadherin+ cells across all tumor sections (independent of treatment) and found a significant inverse correlation for both CD8 T- and NK cells (r2=−0.3, p=0.038 and r2=−0.33, p=0.026, respectively), but not CD4 T-cells (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of multiplex immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The hypoactive NKG2D- NK population (NKNKG2D-ve) is responsible for correlation of NK cells with E-cadherin loss.
claims.source: Surprisingly, the correlation of NK cells with decreased frequency of E-cadherin+ cells was completely abrogated with selection for more functionally competent NK cells (NKActive), implying that the opposite hypoactive NKG2D- NK population (NKNKG2D-ve) is responsible for correlation of NK cells with E-cadherin loss and indeed, a superior inverse correlation is observed for NKNKG2D-ve and E-cadherin compared to NKActive or NKTotal (r2=0.52, p=0.003) (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of multiplex immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: CD8 T-cells significantly segregated with E-cadherinlow tumors.
claims.source: To explore this association is relation to tumor control, sections were split into either E-cadherinhigh or E-cadherinlow and the extent of immune involvement was represented as a percentage of total DAPI+. While CD8 T-cells significantly segregated with E-cadherinlow, implying a contribution to tumor control, the association of NKNKG2D-ve was vastly more significant (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of multiplex immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: More than two-thirds of tumor-infiltrating NK cells expressed the canonical markers of tissue residency CD103 and CD49a after IR/CCR5i/αPD1 treatment.
claims.source: Using a combination of uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) dimensionality reduction and manual gating, we found that more than two-thirds of tumor-infiltrating NK cells expressed the canonical markers of tissue residency CD103 and CD49a (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F), with the double positive population (hereafter referred to as bona fide trNK cells) being barely detectable in untreated mice and rising nearly 40-fold after treatment (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: trNK cells were less likely to be activated and expressed significantly lower levels of NKG2D and NKp46, as well as significantly higher levels of TIM-3.
claims.source: We then compared these two clusters and found that trNK were less likely to be activated and expressed significantly lower levels of the activating receptors NKG2D and NKp46, as well as significantly higher levels of the inhibitory receptor TIM-3 (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: NK cells infiltrating tumors of mice treated with IR/CCR5i/αPD1 were predominantly tissue resident and hypoactive.
claims.source: In line with our multiplex IF data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), these data indicate that NK cells infiltrating tumors of mice treated with the IR/CCR5i/αPD1 combination were predominantly tissue resident and hypoactive, with a minority displaying a more conventional, fully active phenotype.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: UMAP of the CD8 and NK compartment led to three clear NK subpopulations: hypoactive (NK_C1), fully active (NK_C2), and cytotoxic (NK_C3) NK cells.
claims.source: Therefore, we focused on UMAP of the CD8 and NK compartment alone, which led to three clear NK subpopulations that are distinct from CD8 T-cells and clearly separate out in clusters of hypoactive (NK_C1), fully active (NK_C2), and cytotoxic (NK_C3) NK cells from T-cells (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: NKG2D (KLRK1) expression was below detection across all CD8 and NK subpopulations retrieved from patient tumors.
claims.source: In agreement with downregulation of circulating NKG2D+ in PDAC patients, NKG2D (KLRK1) expression was below detection across all CD8 and NK subpopulations retrieved from patient tumors (Groh et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis and a citation to Groh et al., 2002.

claims.claim: The NK_C1 cluster correlates best with the tissue-resident, hypoactive NK phenotype observed in mice.
claims.source: The NK_C1 cluster correlates best with the tissue-resident, hypoactive NK phenotype observed in mice as they similarly displayed reduced cytolytic (reduced NKG7, NKp80, GZMA, and PRF1) with additional expression of tissue residency markers CD103, CD49a, and the adaptive activating receptor NKG2C (KLRC2) (Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of scRNA-seq data with mouse model data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claims.claim: The hypoactive NK_C1 cluster is enriched for CD56 but not CD16 expression.
claims.source: Given that CD56 expression correlates with increased survival in PDAC patients (Figure 1C), we were intrigued to notice that the hypoactive NK_C1 cluster is enriched for CD56 but not CD16 expression (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The NK_C1 cluster represents a subset of NK cells in PDAC that display tissue residency markers and have an immune-secretory phenotype as opposed to cytotoxic phenotype.
claims.source: These data suggest that the NK_C1 cluster represents a subset of NK cells in PDAC that display tissue residency markers (ITGAE, CD103 and ITGA1, CD49a) and have an immune-secretory phenotype (XCL1) as opposed to cytotoxic phenotype (NK_C2 CD16+, NKG7+) (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: The NK_C1 population had the highest expression of the chemokines XCL1 and XCL2.
claims.source: The NK_C1 population had the highest expression of the chemokines XCL1 and XCL2, which have been demonstrated to attract cDC1 (Böttcher et al., 2018) and thereby increase cross-presentation to CD8+ T-cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by scRNA-seq data and a citation to Böttcher et al., 2018.

claims.claim: cDC1 cells are XCR1+ enriched compared to other DC subsets.
claims.source: We next explored myeloid populations in the Steele et al. scPDAC dataset (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and identified cDC1 cells as XCR1+ enriched compared to other DC subsets (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: NK_C1-derived XCL1/2 is the strongest signal to XCR1+ cDC1s.
claims.source: We next employed the R package 'CellChat' (Jin et al., 2021) to further dissect the crosstalk between NK_C1 and other cells found in the pancreatic tumor microenvironment. We again observed that NK_C1-derived XCL1/2 is the strongest signal to XCR1+ cDC1s (Figure 6C), supporting active crosstalk between NK_C1 and cDC1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Among the outgoing signals from different cell types, NK_C1 cells contributed the highest IL-16, CSF, LIGHT (TNFSF14), FASLG, and MIF signals in tumors.
claims.source: Among the outgoing signals from different cell types, NK_C1 cells contributed the highest IL-16, CSF, LIGHT (TNFSF14), FASLG, and MIF signals in tumors (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: There is a highly significant positive association between trNK and CD8 T infiltration in the murine orthotopic tumor model.
claims.source: To support this hypothesis, we explored the correlation between trNK and CD8 T infiltration in our murine orthotopic tumor model and found a highly significant positive association (R²=0.6571, p=0.003), which was strengthened when we focused on untreated (Mock) vs IR+IT combinations where trNK cells are evident (R²=0.9223, p=0.0004) (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: PDAC patient tumors with the highest levels of cDC1s show a strong highly significant correlation between trNK_C1 and CD8A/CD8B.
claims.source: PDAC patient tumors with the lowest evidence for cDC1 involvement had a weak correlation of trNK_C1 with CD8A and CD8B (p=0.047; p=0.045, respectively) which rises to a strong highly significant correlation when the highest levels of cDC1s are present (R=0.55, trNK_C1 vs CD8A p=0.0001; R=0.58, trNK_C1 vs CD8B p=0.000047) (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: The benefit in overall survival of PDAC patients receiving radiotherapy is only apparent in the CD56low patient group.
claims.source: Indeed, separating PAAD_TCGA patients into those who received radiotherapy (RTx) vs those that did not showed that the benefit in overall survival of PDAC patients is only apparent in the CD56low patient group (log-rank p<0.0001, Figure 7).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Patients with tumors enriched for the trNK cell (NK_C1) gene signature were associated with improved PDAC survival.
claims.source: Analysis of primary PDAC tumors from the TCGA (TCGA_PAAD) demonstrates that patients with tumors enriched for the trNK cell (NK_C1) gene signature were associated with improved PDAC survival compared to patients without trNK involvement (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 7 and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Patients with trNKlow benefit from radiotherapy.
claims.source: Similarly to CD56low patients, we find that patients with trNKlow benefit from RTx (log-rank p<0.005, Figure 7).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: CCL5high patients are significantly enriched for the trNK_C1 gene signature.
claims.source: Notably, we find that despite an overall poor prognosis, CCL5high patients (TCGA and CPTAC3) are significantly enriched for the trNK_C1 gene signature (Figure 7), potentially due to strong CCR5 or CCR1-mediated recruitment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TCGA and CPTAC3 data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: CCL5high patients enriched for the NK_C1 signature or CD56 had significantly improved overall and disease-free survival.
claims.source: Indeed, CCL5high patients enriched for the NK_C1 signature or CD56 had significantly improved overall and disease-free survival (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The majority of cancers with enriched expression of the NK_C1 gene signature showed improved survival.
claims.source: The majority of cancers with enriched expression of our NK_C1 gene signature showed improved survival (Figure 8) (apart from endometrium and prostate) as a continuous variable or as a high vs low in a univariate Cox regression (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by pan-cancer survival analysis shown in Figure 8 and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Enrichment of trNK cells is a protective factor across most solid malignancies.
claims.source: The latter result supports our hypothesis that enrichment of trNK cells is a protective factor across most solid malignancies.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from pan-cancer survival analysis.

claims.claim: trNK cells generally improve overall survival through improving CD8 T-cell activity in solid cancers.
claims.source: Moreover, the ability to enrich for this population with IR+IT combinatorial strategies supports the idea that trNK cells generally improve overall survival though improving CD8 T-cell activity in solid cancers.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Combining immune checkpoint inhibitors with inhibitors of myeloid suppression (e.g. CXCR2) failed to impact survival in clinical trials despite showing promise in preclinical studies.
claims.source: Combining them with inhibitors of myeloid suppression (e.g. CXCR2) to increase CD8 T penetration also failed to impact survival in clinical trials despite showing promise in preclinical studies (Steele et al., 2015, Siolas et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Steele et al., 2015 and Siolas et al., 2020.

claims.claim: High-dose hypo-fractionated ablative radiotherapy in conjunction with PD1/PDL1 blockade has not shown benefit in PDAC.
claims.source: Similarly, high-dose hypo-fractionated ablative radiotherapy has been employed to create an acute localized inflammatory response to stimulate intra-tumoral penetration of CD8 T-cells, but even in conjunction with PD1/PDL1 blockade this approach has not shown benefit in PDAC (Parikh et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Parikh et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Novel strategies in preclinical PDAC models comprising IR, αPD1, and BMS-687681 (a dual CCR2/CCR5i) have shown promising increases in CD8 T-cells.
claims.source: Novel strategies in preclinical PDAC models comprising IR, αPD1, and BMS-687681 (a dual CCR2/CCR5i) have shown promising increases in CD8 T-cells (Wang et al., 2022), whereas the combination of IR and the bifunctional agent αPD-1/IL-2Rβγ stimulates tumor penetration of polyfunctional stem-like activated CD8 T-cells and DNAM1+ cytotoxic NK cells (Piper et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2022 and Piper et al., 2023.

claims.claim: The use of IR alongside αPD-1/IL-2Rβγ or FAKi appeared to induce durable immunity in preclinical models.
claims.source: In support of this, the use of IR alongside αPD-1/IL-2Rβγ or FAKi appeared to induce durable immunity in preclinical models (Lander et al., 2022; Piper et al., 2023), suggesting the induction of immunologic memory against tumor antigens is possible.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lander et al., 2022 and Piper et al., 2023.

claims.claim: NK infiltration has been associated with positive outcomes in many solid tumors.
claims.source: NK infiltration has been associated with positive outcomes in many solid tumors, considered to be due to the positive impact of cytotoxic NK cells in cytotoxic CD8 T-mediated tumor clearance (Nersesian et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nersesian et al., 2021.

claims.claim: In melanoma, NK-mediated expression of XCL1 is crucial for the migration of XCR1+ cDC1.
claims.source: In melanoma, NK-mediated expression of XCL1 is crucial for the migration of XCR1+ cDC1 and therefore the non-cytotoxic NK subsets in tumors may be vital for cDC1-mediated cross-presentation of tumor antigens to CD8 T-cells (Böttcher et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Böttcher et al., 2018.

claims.claim: NK-derived FLT3L correlated with increased cDC1 infiltration and improved overall survival and enhanced αPD1 treatment responses in melanoma.
claims.source: NK-derived FLT3L correlated with increased cDC1 infiltration and improved overall survival and enhanced αPD1 treatment responses in melanoma (Barry et al., 2018), while intra-tumoral NK cells correlate with increased T-cell and dendritic cell infiltration and improved survival in neuroblastoma (Melaiu et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barry et al., 2018 and Melaiu et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Reduction of cancer cells correlates with intra-tumoral infiltration of NK cells (CD56brightCD16-) and improved CD8 T-cell penetration in solid tumors.
claims.source: As frequently observed in solid tumors, reduction of cancer cells correlates with intra-tumoral infiltration of NK cells (CD56brightCD16-) and improved CD8 T-cell penetration (Wu et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Adaptive NK cells were first identified as a subpopulation of blood-derived CD16+ NK cells in response to viral infection.
claims.source: Adaptive NK cells were first identified as a subpopulation of blood-derived CD16+ NK cells in response to viral infection but more recently found to be independent of CD16 expression in lung tissue (Brownlie et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brownlie et al., 2021.

claims.claim: trNK-like cells with similar traits are increasingly being observed across a variety of cancers.
claims.source: Likewise, trNK-like cells with similar traits are increasingly being observed across a variety of cancers (Brownlie et al., 2023; Kirchhammer et al., 2022; Marquardt et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brownlie et al., 2023, Kirchhammer et al., 2022, and Marquardt et al., 2015.

claims.claim: CD56 (NCAM1) is a key marker that represents functionally distinct subpopulations of NK cells.
claims.source: CD56 (NCAM1) is a key marker that represents functionally distinct subpopulations of NK cells where CD56bright NK cells represent immature states that move to CD56dim upon maturation to full cytotoxic potential, whereas conversely CD16+ expression marks activation and CD16- immature or quiescent NK cells (Poli et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Poli et al., 2009.

claims.claim: IL-16 is mainly known as a chemoattractant for CD4+ T-cells.
claims.source: IL-16 is mainly known as a chemoattractant for CD4+ T-cells, however CD4+ dendritic cells have also been demonstrated to be recruited by IL-16 (Bialecki et al., 2011; Kaser et al., 1999; Vremec et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bialecki et al., 2011, Kaser et al., 1999, and Vremec et al., 2000.

claims.claim: IL-16 has the potential to induce MHC antigen presentation in CD4+ cells.
claims.source: IL-16 has also been described to increase HLA-DR levels in CD4+ T-cells and eosinophils, indicating that it has the potential to induce MHC antigen presentation in CD4+ cells (Cruikshank et al., 1987; Rand et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cruikshank et al., 1987 and Rand et al., 1991.

claims.claim: Dendritic cell-secreted BAG6 could promote both survival and cytokine release of NK cells by binding to NKp30.
claims.source: On the other hand, dendritic cell-secreted BAG6 could promote both survival and cytokine release of NK cells by binding to NKp30 (Simhadri et al., 2008) and directly signal to CD8 T-cells via CXCL16-CXCR6 (Di Pilato et al., 2021; Vella et al., 2021), thereby generating an anti-tumor feedforward loop (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Simhadri et al., 2008, Di Pilato et al., 2021, and Vella et al., 2021.

claims.claim: IL-16 could contribute to immunosuppression via enhanced Treg migration and expansion.
claims.source: IL-16 also communicates to CD4+ Tregs, which could contribute to immunosuppression via enhanced Treg migration and expansion (Figure 6D; McFadden et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McFadden et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Tregs may be susceptible to Fas-mediated cell death due to NK_C1 expression of Fas ligand.
claims.source: However, Tregs may also be susceptible to Fas-mediated cell death due to NK_C1 expression of Fas ligand (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The inactivation of cytotoxic NK cells in tumors appears to be a conversion to immunomodulatory trNKs.
claims.source: Moreover, this supports a model where the inactivation of cytotoxic NK cells in tumors appears to be a conversion to immunomodulatory trNKs and perhaps an important mechanistic switch from innate to adaptive immunity.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: IR/CCR5i/αPD1 offers a potential regimen to increase disease-free survival in PDAC.
claims.source: Our therapeutic combination strategy of short ablative radiation-induced damage (IR) followed by CCR5i/αPD1 (IT) offers a potential regimen to increase disease-free survival in PDAC.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: CCL5-mediated recruitment of NK cells can be beneficial in the absence of CCL5-CCR5 recruitment, likely via CCR1 signaling.
claims.source: This also supports a model where CCL5-mediated recruitment of NK cells can be beneficial in the absence of CCL5-CCR5 recruitment, likely via CCR1 signaling (Ajuebor et al., 2007; Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data and supported by a citation to Ajuebor et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Despite high CCL5 levels and an overall poor prognostic outcome, the presence of trNK cells significantly improves survival.
claims.source: These results suggest that despite high CCL5 levels and an overall poor prognostic outcome, the presence of trNK cells significantly improves survival and provides an opportunity for intervention with the IR+IT combination.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the survival analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The reduced NKG2D expression on NK cells may be a result of prolonged engagement by ligands expressed on tumor cells, followed by ligand-induced endocytosis and degradation.
claims.source: The reduced NKG2D expression on NK cells may be a result of the prolonged engagement by ligands expressed on tumor cells, followed by ligand-induced endocytosis and degradation (Quatrini et al., 2015), or the shedding of NKG2D ligands by tumor cells (Kaiser et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citations to Quatrini et al., 2015 and Kaiser et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Circulating NK cells from PDAC patients show reduced NKG2D levels compared to healthy controls.
claims.source: Moreover, circulating NK cells from PDAC patients show reduced NKG2D levels compared to healthy controls (Peng et al., 2013) supporting the notion that chronic exposure to NKG2D ligands expressed or shed by PDAC cells might cause NKG2D down-modulation and a hypo-responsive phenotype.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Peng et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Receptor downregulation causes a reduction in cytotoxicity and impairs NK cell responsiveness to tumor cells, potentially contributing to exhaustion.
claims.source: In both instances, receptor downregulation causes a reduction in cytotoxicity and impairs NK cell responsiveness to tumor cells, potentially contributing to exhaustion (Groh et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Groh et al., 2002.

claims.claim: trNK cells may improve tumor control via recruitment of cDC1 via XCR1, while promoting DC maturation via LIGHT-CD86 signaling and supporting DC antigen presentation to both CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells via MIF-CD74 signaling.
claims.source: Taken together, these interactions support the hypothesis that trNK cells may improve tumor control via recruitment of cDC1 via XCR1, while promoting DC maturation via LIGHT-CD86 signaling (Zou and Hu, 2005) and supporting DC antigen presentation to both CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells via MIF-CD74 signaling (Basha et al., 2012; Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from CellChat analysis and supported by citations to Zou and Hu, 2005 and Basha et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Patients with CCL5high NK_C1low would perform significantly worse than patients with CCL5highNK_C1high.
claims.source: Therefore, we would expect that patients with CCL5high NK_C1low would perform significantly worse than patients with CCL5highNK_C1high.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The benefit of CD56 can be attributed to NK cells over neuronal expression as the neuronal cell-specific homolog NCAM2 has no prognostic value.
claims.source: The benefit of CD56 can be attributed to NK cells over neuronal expression as the neuronal cell-specific homolog NCAM2 has no prognostic value (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Pancreatic tissue NK_C1 cells could comprise, at least in part, adaptive-like trNK cells.
claims.source: While adaptive NK cells in the peripheral circulation are associated with a CD56dimCD16+ phenotype, adaptive-like (i.e. NKG2C+) CD56brightCD16dim trNK cells have been identified in other epithelial sites such as the lungs (Brownlie et al., 2021), therefore, our pancreatic tissue NK_C1 cells could comprise, at least in part, adaptive-like trNK cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data and supported by a citation to Brownlie et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Verification of the NK_C1 population as trNK cells in a second scRNA-seq pancreatic cancer dataset of Peng et al., 2013, further supports the existence of these hypoactive cells in an independent PDAC cohort.
claims.source: Verification of the NK_C1 population as trNK cells in a second scRNA-seq pancreatic cancer dataset of Peng et al., 2013, further supports the existence of these hypoactive cells in an independent PDAC cohort (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of a second scRNA-seq dataset shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F.

claims.claim: The TNFSF14 (LIGHT)-TNFRSF14 pair was the most universal intercellular interaction between NK_C1 and other cell groups.
claims.source: Analysis of specific ligand-receptor pairs between NK_C1 and 24 other cell groups yielded 32 significant interactions, of which the TNFSF14 (LIGHT)-TNFRSF14 pair was the most universal intercellular interaction, whereas CD74 (or MIF) signaling showed the highest communication probability (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Communication signals between NK_C1 and macrophages were the most abundant and diverse within the immune cell compartment.
claims.source: Within the immune cell compartment, communication signals between NK_C1 and macrophages were the most abundant and diverse, followed by cDCs (cDC2 and cDC1) and Tregs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: cDC1 in PDAC samples seem capable of presenting MHC class I peptides to CD8+ T-cells, but also MHC class II to CD4+ Tregs.
claims.source: Similarly, cDC1 in these PDAC samples also seem capable of presenting MHC class I peptides to CD8+ T-cells, but surprisingly also MHC class II to CD4+ Tregs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: KPC-F is an appropriate model for human PDAC tumor based on the expression of epithelial, mesenchymal, and stromal markers as well as displaying growth kinetics amenable for the study.
claims.source: From a selection of independently isolated KPC-derived cell lines, we first determined the cell line KPC-F as an appropriate model for human PDAC tumor based on the expression of epithelial (E-cadherin), mesenchymal (vimentin), and stromal (Collagen I, αSMA) markers as well as displaying growth kinetics (determined by MRI) amenable for the study and expression of high levels of CCL5 (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental characterization data shown in Figure 2A and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Pilot experiments injecting 500 KPC-F cells yielded robust and replicative growth kinetics.
claims.source: Pilot experiments injecting 500 KPC-F cells yielded robust and replicative growth kinetics (indicated by matching volumes of ±100 mm3 at the beginning of exponential growth), permitting direct comparisons of infiltrating immune cells across different treatment groups (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Responses to combination of IR with CCR5i, αPD1, or CCR5i+αPD1 showed larger variations compared to IR alone, implying mixtures of 'responders' and 'non-responders' to immune-modulatory treatments.
claims.source: Responses to combination of IR with CCR5i, αPD1, or CCR5i+αPD1 (IR+IT) showed larger variations compared to IR alone, implying mixtures of 'responders' and 'non-responders' to immune-modulatory treatments.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from tumor growth data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The triple combination reduced PMN-MDSC infiltration.
claims.source: Interestingly, no alteration was seen in the myeloid compartment, except for a reduced infiltration of PMN-MDSCs, whereas a significant infiltration of NK and NKT cells could be observed in pairwise comparisons between IR+αPD1 vs IR+CCR5i or IR/CCR5i/αPD1 (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The triple combination treatment demonstrated a significant overall reduction in E-cadherin+ tumor cells as a percentage of total DAPI+ cells.
claims.source: Notably, despite having responders and non-responders in the combination groups (Figure 4A), a significant overall reduction in E-cadherin+ tumor cells as a percentage of total DAPI+ cells was observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), supporting a decrease in cellularity and an increase in tumor necrosis with the IR/CCR5i/αPD1 combination (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiplex immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The increase in CD8+ T-cells with combination treatment appears independent of tumor area and is matched by a similar increase in NK cells.
claims.source: The increase in CD8+ T-cells with combination treatment appears independent of tumor area and is matched by a similar increase in NK cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiplex immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claims.claim: The proportion of infiltrating CD3-NK1.1+NKG2D+ cells (NKActive) in stained tissue sections was reduced under IR/CCR5iαPD1 combination treatment.
claims.source: Surprisingly, the proportion of infiltrating CD3-NK1.1+NKG2D+ cells (NKActive) in stained tissue sections was reduced under IR/CCR5iαPD1 combination treatment, implying a decrease in total NK cell cytotoxic capacity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiplex immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The reciprocal CD3-NK1.1+NKG2D- population increases upon triple combination treatment.
claims.source: Indeed, the reciprocal CD3-NK1.1+NKG2D- population increases upon triple combination treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiplex immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The double positive CD103+CD49a+ population (bona fide trNK cells) was barely detectable in untreated mice and rose nearly 40-fold after treatment.
claims.source: Using a combination of uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) dimensionality reduction and manual gating, we found that more than two-thirds of tumor-infiltrating NK cells expressed the canonical markers of tissue residency CD103 and CD49a (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F), with the double positive population (hereafter referred to as bona fide trNK cells) being barely detectable in untreated mice and rising nearly 40-fold after treatment (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: CD16high (FCGR3a) cytolytic NK cells (NK_C3) cluster separately from CD16- NK cells (NK_C1) which are more enriched for genes related to cytokine secretion than cytolytic function.
claims.source: As expected, CD16high (FCGR3a) cytolytic NK cells (NK_C3) cluster separately from CD16- NK cells (NK_C1) which are more enriched for genes related to cytokine secretion than cytolytic function (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: A core signature gene set distinguishes NK_C1 from other NK subpopulations.
claims.source: Furthermore, we defined a core signature gene set to distinguish NK_C1 from other NK subpopulations (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Downstream UMAP analysis of the NK cell population distinguishes three subsets of NK cells (NK_C1, NK_C2, and NK_C3) based on 41 differentially expressed genes.
claims.source: Downstream UMAP analysis of the NK cell population distinguishes these three subsets of NK cells (NK_C1, NK_C2, and NK_C3) based on 41 differentially expressed genes (Figure 5D and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D and E.

results.result: CCL5 is a negative prognostic marker in pancreatic cancer, with higher expression associating with poor overall and disease-free survival in independent PDAC cohorts.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 are supported by prior work (Willenbrock et al., 2021) and validated in two independent cohorts (CPTAC3 and TCGA) with survival data shown in Figure 1A. The consistency across multiple datasets strengthens the finding.

results.result: CCL5-CCR5 signaling promotes an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment in pancreatic cancer, and CCR5 inhibition reduces tumor cell migration, invasiveness, and Treg recruitment in preclinical models.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C7 are supported by multiple citations to prior work establishing the role of CCL5-CCR5 signaling in recruiting immunosuppressive cells and the effects of CCR5 inhibition. These represent established knowledge and prior findings rather than new results from this study.

results.result: The KPC-F cell line is an appropriate model for human PDAC with high CCL5 expression, and CCR5i treatment significantly reduces Treg infiltration in orthotopic tumors.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C23, C86, and C87 are supported by experimental characterization data (Figure 2A, supplementary figures) and flow cytometry data (Figure 2B). The model validation and Treg reduction are well-documented, though sample sizes and statistical details could be more explicit.

results.result: CCR5i alone restricts Treg involvement but does not therapeutically benefit tumor viability alone or with αPD1, and is unlikely to clinically benefit PDAC progression as a standalone treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C13, and C24 are supported by experimental data from the murine model showing limited efficacy of CCR5i monotherapy. The inference about clinical benefit (C24) is reasonable based on the tumor growth data, though it remains speculative for human application.

results.result: IR/CCR5i/αPD1 triple combination treatment results in significant tumor control with reduced tumor cells, increased necrosis, enhanced CD8+ T-cell infiltration, reduced Tregs, and increased NK/NKT cell infiltration.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C25-C29, and C89 are supported by multiple complementary data types (IHC, flow cytometry, histology) shown in Figures 3B-E and supplementary figures. The convergence of evidence from different methodologies strengthens these findings, though variability in treatment response (responders vs non-responders) is noted.

results.result: CD8 T-cells and hypoactive NKG2D- NK cells show significant inverse correlation with E-cadherin+ tumor cells, with NKG2D- NK cells showing superior correlation with tumor control compared to active NK cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32 are supported by correlation analysis of multiplex immunofluorescence data (Figures 4B-D). The finding that hypoactive NK cells correlate better with tumor control than active NK cells is counterintuitive but well-documented with statistical support (r²=0.52, p=0.003).

results.result: IR/CCR5i/αPD1 treatment induces tissue-resident NK (trNK) cells expressing CD103+CD49a+ that are hypoactive with reduced NKG2D and NKp46 expression and increased TIM-3 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35, C92-C94 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figures 4E-F, supplementary figures) showing a nearly 40-fold increase in CD103+CD49a+ NK cells after treatment with characteristic hypoactive phenotype. The phenotypic characterization is thorough and consistent across multiple markers.

results.result: Human PDAC tumors contain three distinct NK subpopulations (NK_C1, NK_C2, NK_C3), with NK_C1 representing tissue-resident, hypoactive NK cells enriched for CD56 but not CD16, displaying an immune-secretory rather than cytotoxic phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40, C95-C97 are supported by scRNA-seq analysis of human PDAC samples (Figures 5A-F). The identification of NK subpopulations and their characterization is well-documented, though the correlation with mouse model findings (C38) involves some inference. The absence of NKG2D expression across all populations is noted.

results.result: NK_C1 cells express high levels of XCL1/XCL2 chemokines that signal to XCR1+ cDC1 cells, and contribute the highest IL-16, CSF, LIGHT, FASLG, and MIF signals in tumors, with most abundant communication to macrophages within the immune compartment.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44, C83-C84 are supported by scRNA-seq data and CellChat analysis (Figures 6A-D, supplementary figures). The ligand-receptor interaction analysis is comprehensive, identifying 32 significant interactions with detailed characterization of signaling pathways.

results.result: trNK cells correlate with CD8 T-cell infiltration in both mouse models and human PDAC in a cDC1-dependent manner, with correlation strength increasing with cDC1 levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C45, C46, and C17 are supported by correlation analysis in mouse models (Figure 6F, R²=0.9223, p=0.0004 for treated groups) and human TCGA data (Figure 6G) showing cDC1-dependent correlation. The stratification by cDC1 levels strengthens the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: trNK cells may improve tumor control through a complex signaling network involving recruitment of cDC1 via XCR1, DC maturation via LIGHT-CD86, antigen presentation support via MIF-CD74, and potential Treg elimination via FasL, while cDC1 can present antigens to both CD8+ T-cells and CD4+ Tregs.
results.evaluation: Claims C78, C68-C70, and C85 are based on inference from CellChat analysis and supported by citations to prior work. While the signaling pathways are well-documented individually, the integrated model of trNK-mediated tumor control involves substantial speculation. The dual role of cDC1 in presenting to both effector T-cells and Tregs (C85) adds complexity. Experimental validation of this proposed mechanism is needed.

results.result: Radiotherapy benefit in PDAC patients is only apparent in CD56low and trNKlow patient groups, while patients with tumors enriched for trNK signature show improved survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 are supported by survival analysis of TCGA data (Figure 7) showing significant stratification by CD56 and trNK signature with radiotherapy. The finding that low trNK/CD56 patients benefit from radiotherapy while high trNK patients have better baseline survival is internally consistent and statistically significant.

results.result: CCL5high patients are enriched for trNK signature and show improved survival when trNK levels are high, supporting a model where CCL5-mediated NK recruitment via CCR1 (not CCR5) can be beneficial.
results.evaluation: Claims C50, C51, C73, C74, and C79 are supported by analysis of TCGA and CPTAC3 data (Figure 7) showing that CCL5high/trNKhigh patients have better outcomes than CCL5high/trNKlow patients. The proposed CCR1-mediated mechanism (C73) is supported by citation and receptor expression data, though C79 remains a prediction requiring validation.

results.result: The trNK (NK_C1) gene signature associates with improved survival across most solid malignancies (14 tumor types), supporting that trNK enrichment is a protective factor that improves overall survival through enhancing CD8 T-cell activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 and C18 are supported by pan-cancer survival analysis (Figure 8, supplementary figures) showing improved survival in the majority of cancer types (exceptions: endometrium and prostate). The consistency across multiple cancer types strengthens the generalizability, though the mechanistic claim (C54) involves inference from the combined data.

results.result: The inactivation of cytotoxic NK cells in tumors represents a conversion to immunomodulatory trNKs, and IR/CCR5i/αPD1 offers a potential therapeutic regimen to increase disease-free survival in PDAC.
results.evaluation: Claims C71 and C72 represent speculative interpretations and future therapeutic potential based on the data. While the data support the presence and beneficial association of trNK cells, the mechanistic model of NK cell conversion (C71) and the clinical therapeutic potential (C72) require prospective validation. These are reasonable hypotheses but not definitively proven.

results.result: Reduced NKG2D expression on NK cells in PDAC may result from prolonged ligand engagement or ligand shedding by tumor cells, leading to receptor downregulation, reduced cytotoxicity, and potential NK cell exhaustion.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are supported by citations to prior work (Quatrini et al., 2015; Kaiser et al., 2007; Peng et al., 2013; Groh et al., 2002) and consistent with the observed NKG2D- phenotype in the study. While C75 involves speculation about mechanism, it is well-grounded in established literature.

results.result: The beneficial prognostic effect of CD56 can be attributed to NK cells rather than neuronal expression, and the pancreatic NK_C1 cells may comprise adaptive-like trNK cells similar to those found in lung tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 are supported by data showing NCAM2 has no prognostic value (Figure 1 supplement 1C), expression of NKG2C in NK_C1 cells, and validation in a second scRNA-seq dataset (Figure 5 supplement 1E-F). The comparison to lung trNK cells (C81) is reasonable but involves some inference.

results.result: IR combined with immunotherapy shows variable responses (responders vs non-responders) but overall demonstrates significant reduction in E-cadherin+ tumor cells and increased immune cell infiltration independent of tumor area.
results.evaluation: Claims C88, C90, and C91 are supported by multiplex immunofluorescence data (Figure 4A, supplementary figures) showing heterogeneous responses but overall significant effects. The acknowledgment of response heterogeneity is important for interpreting the data, though the biological basis for this variability is not explored.

results.result: Prior work in NSCLC identified tissue-resident memory CD8+ T-cells and showed that IL-12-induced trNK cells support cDC1 infiltration and DC-CD8+ T-cell interactions in a CCL5-dependent manner when combined with PD1 blockade.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C11 accurately summarize prior work from Caushi et al., 2021 and Kirchhammer et al., 2022. These provide important context for the current study but represent background rather than new findings. The citations appear appropriate and the interpretations are reasonable.

results.result: Prior clinical and preclinical studies show limited success of immunotherapy in PDAC due to the immunosuppressive microenvironment, though novel combination strategies show promise in preclinical models.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 and C55-C58 accurately summarize the clinical context and prior work with appropriate citations. These establish the rationale for the current study but do not represent new findings. The summary of prior work appears accurate and comprehensive.

results.result: Prior work establishes that NK infiltration associates with positive outcomes in solid tumors, with non-cytotoxic NK subsets playing important roles in recruiting cDC1 and supporting adaptive immunity through various signaling mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C67 provide comprehensive background on NK cell biology and prior findings with appropriate citations. These establish the conceptual framework for interpreting the current findings but represent established knowledge rather than new results. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are accurate.

results.result: CCL5 expression is a negative prognostic marker in PDAC, with higher CCL5 levels associating with poor overall and disease-free survival in independent cohorts (CPTAC3 and TCGA).
results.evaluation: All reviewers accept these claims without challenge. Reviewer 3 explicitly acknowledges 'CCL5 expression within the tumor microenvironment negatively correlated with clinical outcomes in human patients with PDAC' as one of the key observations. No concerns are raised about this finding.

results.result: CCR5i alone significantly reduces Treg infiltration in orthotopic PDAC tumors but does not therapeutically benefit tumor viability alone or together with αPD1, making standalone CCR5 inhibition unlikely to clinically benefit PDAC progression.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a critical concern: 'The role of CCR5i requires further clarification/discussion. While the authors demonstrated its capacity to reduce Treg in murine tumors, its impact on other cell populations, including NK cells and CD8+ T cells, was not observed. Nevertheless, the effect of CCR5i on tumor growth in Figure 2B seems pathogenic. If the combination of radiotherapy and αPD1 already can achieve good outcomes as shown in Figure 3A, the necessity to include CCR5i is questioned.' This indicates uncertainty about the role and necessity of CCR5i.

results.result: IR/CCR5i/αPD1 triple combination treatment results in significant alterations in immune infiltration (reduced Tregs and PMN-MDSCs, increased NK, NKT, and CD8+ T-cells), reduced tumor cellularity, increased necrosis, and better tumor control compared to other treatment conditions.
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 states the work 'convincingly illustrates how irradiation combined with CCR5i and PD1 blockade leads to a reduction in pancreatic cancer growth that correlates with a reduction in Treg cells and enhancement of NK and CD8 T cells in the TME.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'CCR5 inhibition augmented anti-PD1 immunotherapy when combined with ionizing radiation (IR) therapy in the murine model' and notes 'the above therapy resulted in increased infiltration of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells.' Despite concerns about CCR5i alone, the triple combination effect is accepted.

results.result: IR/CCR5i/αPD1 combination treatment induces a tissue-resident NK (trNK) population characterized by CD103+CD49a+ expression, hypoactive phenotype (NKG2D-, NKp46low, TIM-3high), and this NKG2D- NK population shows superior inverse correlation with E-cadherin+ tumor cells compared to active NK cells or CD8 T-cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding. Reviewer 1 notes 'The work convincingly illustrates...enhancement of NK and CD8 T cells in the TME.' Reviewer 3 explicitly acknowledges the identification of 'a subset of NKG2D-negative, tissue-residency (tr) marker expressing NK cells (deemed Cluster 1 NK in their data sets) that inversely correlated with the number of E-cadherin+ cells (i.e. tumor cells).' No methodological concerns are raised about these observations.

results.result: An equivalent trNK population (NK_C1) exists in human PDAC scRNA-seq datasets, characterized by tissue residency markers (CD103, CD49a), hypoactive phenotype (reduced cytolytic markers, NKG2D below detection), CD56bright/CD16- expression, and high XCL1/XCL2 expression, representing immunomodulatory cells that support cDC1-CD8 communication.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 states the manuscript 'provides an interesting account documenting the role of resident CD56(br) NK cells in driving interaction with dendritic cells that attract CD8+ T cells to the pancreas cancer tumor microenvironment.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'They identify a specific "hypofunctional" NK cell population in both mouse and human PDAC that supports CD8 T cell involvement.' One minor concern from Reviewer 1: 'it is important to point out that transcripts (not protein expression) of KLRC2 is common in CD56bright NK cells and does not really reflect "adaptive-like" NK cells,' but this does not challenge the core finding.

results.result: CellChat analysis reveals NK_C1 cells as XCR1+ cDC1 recruiters via XCL1/2, with NK_C1 contributing the highest IL-16, CSF, LIGHT, FASLG, and MIF signals, supporting a model where trNK cells improve tumor control via cDC1 recruitment, DC maturation (LIGHT-CD86), and DC antigen presentation support (MIF-CD74).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding. Reviewer 3 explicitly acknowledges 'the authors identified a number of putative signals stemming from the trNK (e.g. IL-16, TNFSF14, FASLG, CSF, MIF) as well as incoming from cDC1s to NK (e.g. BAG6-NKp30)' and notes 'predicted interactions with cDC1 dendritic cells (including XCL1/XCL2 expressed by the NK and XCR1 expressed by the cDC1).' No concerns are raised about the CellChat analysis or interpretation.

results.result: There is a highly significant positive association between trNK and CD8 T infiltration in the murine orthotopic tumor model (R²=0.6571, p=0.003), and in human PDAC patient tumors with high cDC1 levels, there is a strong correlation between trNK_C1 and CD8A/CD8B (R=0.55-0.58, p<0.0001).
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this finding. Reviewer 3 notes 'these trNK cells positively correlated with good outcomes and with CD8+ T cell infiltrations in human PDAC.' Reviewer 2 states 'Subsequent cell-cell contact analysis reveals the NK-cDC1-CD8 cell axis in pancreatic cancer.' The correlation data supporting the trNK-cDC1-CD8 axis is accepted without challenge.

results.result: A trNK (NK_C1) gene signature associates with improved survival in PDAC and other solid malignancies. Patients with low CD56 or low trNK benefit from radiotherapy, while CCL5high patients enriched for NK_C1 signature have significantly improved survival. The majority of cancers with enriched NK_C1 signature show improved survival, supporting that trNK enrichment is a protective factor across most solid malignancies.
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 states 'The correlation of NKC1 signature with survival in pancreatic cancer patients is indeed of broader interest regarding potential relevance to other types of cancer.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the notion that NK C1 signature correlates with patient survival in various solid cancers is of high interest and relevance.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'these trNK cells positively correlated with good outcomes...in human PDAC as well as in many other solid tumor types.' The survival associations are accepted as valid and significant.

results.result: CCL5high patients are significantly enriched for the trNK_C1 gene signature, and despite high CCL5 levels and overall poor prognosis, the presence of trNK cells significantly improves survival. This supports a model where CCL5-mediated recruitment of NK cells can be beneficial in the absence of CCL5-CCR5 recruitment, likely via CCR1 signaling.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding. Reviewer 2 notes 'Human database analysis showed a positive correlation between NK C1 score and CCL5 in pancreatic cancer.' Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'there were both positive and negative correlations between CCL5 expression and the expression of specific genes (e.g. those encoding CD56 and CD16, respectively).' The interpretation that trNK presence improves survival even in CCL5high patients is accepted without challenge.

results.result: KPC-F cells express high levels of CCL5 and represent an appropriate model for human PDAC tumor based on expression of epithelial, mesenchymal, and stromal markers, with robust and replicative growth kinetics amenable for study.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the model characterization. Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'Mouse experiments nicely confirmed that such combined therapy could significantly reduce tumor volume.' The KPC-F model is implicitly accepted as appropriate for the study without specific concerns raised.

results.result: CD8 T-cells and NK cells show significant inverse correlation with E-cadherin+ cells across tumor sections, with the increase in CD8+ T-cells and NK cells appearing independent of tumor area, and a significant overall reduction in E-cadherin+ tumor cells observed with triple combination treatment.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these correlative findings. Reviewer 3 notes 'the above therapy resulted in increased infiltration of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells as well as of a subset of NKG2D-negative, tissue-residency (tr) marker expressing NK cells...that inversely correlated with the number of E-cadherin+ cells (i.e. tumor cells).' The correlation analysis is not challenged.

results.result: Responses to IR+IT combinations showed larger variations implying responders and non-responders. The triple combination reduced PMN-MDSC infiltration, reduced the proportion of NKG2D+ active NK cells, increased the reciprocal NKG2D- population, and induced a 40-fold increase in CD103+CD49a+ bona fide trNK cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these observations. Reviewer 3 notes 'the above therapy resulted in increased infiltration of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells as well as of a subset of NKG2D-negative, tissue-residency (tr) marker expressing NK cells.' The characterization of responders/non-responders and the detailed NK phenotyping are not challenged.

results.result: UMAP analysis of human PDAC NK cells distinguishes three subsets (NK_C1, NK_C2, NK_C3) based on 41 differentially expressed genes, with CD16high cytolytic NK cells (NK_C3) clustering separately from CD16- NK cells (NK_C1) which are enriched for cytokine secretion genes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the scRNA-seq clustering. Reviewer 2 states 'The elegant use of single-cell sequencing analysis and human database examination enriches the narrative and strengthens the study's foundation.' The NK subpopulation identification is not challenged.

results.result: The inactivation of cytotoxic NK cells in tumors appears to be a conversion to immunomodulatory trNKs, representing an important mechanistic switch from innate to adaptive immunity. IR/CCR5i/αPD1 offers a potential regimen to increase disease-free survival in PDAC, and patients with CCL5high NK_C1low would be expected to perform significantly worse than CCL5highNK_C1high patients.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these interpretive conclusions. Reviewer 1 notes the work 'provides an interesting account documenting the role of resident CD56(br) NK cells in driving interaction with dendritic cells.' Reviewer 3 states 'the authors proposed that combining IR with CCR5 inhibition and anti-PD1 immunotherapy is a promising strategy to treat solid cancers' and notes 'the collective analyses and conclusions appear to be novel and could be of high and rapid impact on the field.' The mechanistic interpretation is accepted.

results.result: Background claims about CCL5 biology, PDAC microenvironment, prior therapeutic approaches, NK cell biology, and supporting mechanistic details from the literature.
results.evaluation: These are primarily literature-based background claims supported by citations. Reviewers do not challenge these established concepts. Reviewer 1 notes one minor point: 'it is important to point out that transcripts (not protein expression) of KLRC2 is common in CD56bright NK cells and does not really reflect "adaptive-like" NK cells,' but this is a clarification rather than a challenge to the core background.

results.result: Speculative mechanistic claims about trNK cells improving survival through CD8 T-cell activity and potential Fas-mediated Treg death due to NK_C1 FasL expression.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these as reasonable interpretations. Reviewer 3 notes 'One of the limitations is that the authors did not perform functional in vivo or ex vivo assays to address some of the major hypotheses that arose from the descriptive, correlative data; but overall, this does not detract from the enthusiasm for the work or the potential significance and impact of the study.' The speculative nature is acknowledged but accepted as part of the discussion.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on C1 and C2. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers support the finding that CCL5 expression negatively correlates with clinical outcomes in PDAC patients, validated across multiple cohorts.

Disagreement on C12, C13, C24. OpenEval finds claims supported by experimental data showing limited CCR5i monotherapy efficacy. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, questioning the necessity of CCR5i given its pathogenic effect on tumor growth and lack of impact on NK/CD8+ cells.

Strong agreement on C14, C25-C29. Both evaluations support the triple combination therapy effects (radiation + CCR5i + anti-PD1) showing Treg reduction and enhancement of NK and CD8+ T cells, despite concerns about CCR5i alone.

Agreement on C33-C35. Both support the identification and characterization of CD103+CD49a+ hypoactive NK cells with nearly 40-fold increase after treatment. Peer reviewers affirm the NKG2D-negative, tissue-residency marker expressing NK cell subset.

Agreement on C36-C40, C96. Both support the scRNA-seq identification of NK subpopulations in human PDAC and their correlation with mouse findings. Minor concern from peer reviewer about KLRC2 transcript interpretation not challenging core finding.

Agreement on C42-C44, C83-C84. Both support the CellChat ligand-receptor interaction analysis identifying 32 significant interactions and characterization of signaling pathways between trNK and cDC1 cells.
Agreement on C45-C46. Both support the correlation analysis showing cDC1-dependent relationship between trNK and CD8+ T cells in mouse models and human TCGA data, affirming the trNK-cDC1-CD8 axis.

Agreement on C47-C49. Both support the survival analysis showing trNK signature correlates with outcomes in PDAC and pan-cancer contexts. Peer reviewers emphasize broader interest and high relevance across cancer types.
Agreement on C50, C73-C74. Both support the finding that CCL5high/trNKhigh patients have better outcomes than CCL5high/trNKlow patients, with CCR1-mediated mechanism accepted.

Agreement on C22, C86-C87. Both support the KPC-F murine model characterization and validation, with Treg reduction documented. Peer reviewers implicitly accept model appropriateness without specific concerns.
Agreement on C30. Both support the correlation analysis showing hypoactive NK cells correlate better with tumor control than active NK cells, with statistical support accepted.

Agreement on C88, C90-C91. Both support the multiplex immunofluorescence data showing heterogeneous but overall significant treatment responses, with acknowledgment of responder/non-responder variability.
Agreement on C95, C97. Both support the scRNA-seq clustering and NK subpopulation identification. Peer reviewers praise the elegant use of single-cell sequencing analysis.

Difference in evaluation type on C71-C72. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting these are speculative interpretations requiring validation. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the mechanistic interpretation and therapeutic potential as reasonable conclusions with acknowledged limitations.

Agreement on C3-C7. Both support these as established background knowledge from prior work on CCL5-CCR5 signaling. OpenEval notes these represent established knowledge rather than new findings; peer reviewers accept without challenge.
Agreement on C8-C11. Both support these as accurate summaries of prior work (Caushi et al., 2021; Kirchhammer et al., 2022) providing important context. No challenges to the background literature.
Agreement on C19-C21, C55-C58. Both support these clinical context and prior work claims as accurate background with appropriate citations, not representing new findings.

Agreement on C59-C67. Both support these NK cell biology background claims as established knowledge with appropriate citations. Minor clarification from peer reviewer about KLRC2 does not challenge core background.
Agreement on C75-C77. Both support these claims about NKG2D downregulation as grounded in established literature, consistent with observed phenotype in the study.
Agreement on C80-C82. Both support the validation data showing NCAM2 has no prognostic value, NKG2C expression in NK_C1, and validation in second scRNA-seq dataset.

Partial overlap on C78, C85. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the integrated mechanistic model involves substantial speculation requiring validation. Peer reviewers rate related claims (C42-C44, C83-C84) as SUPPORTED, accepting the CellChat analysis without challenging the mechanistic interpretation.

Partial overlap on C70. OpenEval rates C68-C70 as UNCERTAIN within broader mechanistic speculation. Peer reviewers rate C70 as SUPPORTED, acknowledging speculative nature but accepting as reasonable discussion point with noted limitations.
Agreement on C18, C52-C53. Both support the pan-cancer survival analysis showing improved survival across multiple cancer types. Peer reviewers emphasize broader interest and potential significance.

Partial overlap on C54. OpenEval supports the mechanistic claim as involving inference but well-supported. Peer reviewers accept as reasonable interpretation acknowledging limitations in functional validation.
